title: Information Has Never Been More Abundant, and We Choose Not to Know
dek: Lyse Doucet has reported from war zones for forty years, and her judgment is this: not knowing isn't because there isn't enough information, it's because we don't want to know. And this Iran war is a war of choice, and it has made everything worse.
why: The first half is instant judgment on Iran and Hormuz; the second half is a rare post-mortem on whether twenty years of intervention in Afghanistan was worth it. High information density, but it requires patience.
who: Journalists covering the Middle East and Afghanistan, international relations researchers, humanitarian workers, and readers who want to understand the frameworks of the "war of choice" and "hope vs optimism."
skip: The counterfactual speculation after 1:19:53, which is lower in information density.

points.h: Not knowing is because we don't want to know
points.body: Doucet calls this "a really jarring time": information has never been more abundant, but "If we don't know about something, it's because we don't want to know about something. We choose not to know." She traces the cause to being bombarded every day by statements from the American president — yesterday it was "we don't need guardrails on AI," even though some of the leading founders in AI are asking for regulation; today it's rolling back some environmental regulations. She reminds us: a president who said he wouldn't get into "forever wars" still ended up leading the country into these wars.

points.h: This is a war of choice, and it keeps getting worse
points.body: Doucet rarely offers a personal judgment: this war puts her under great pressure, because it is "a war of choice" rather than "a war of necessity," and "it just seems to have made everything worse in every way." She acknowledges that the US and Israel together have done enormous damage to Iran's military and navy, and that Iran's economy is suffering, but strategically "this is a war where President Trump doesn't know how to end it." Iran has not collapsed, the regime is harder than before, the promises made to the demonstrators have not been kept, and their lives have only gotten worse.

Doucet uses inflation to illustrate Iran's predicament: Britons worry about single-digit inflation, "Oh, 4%, oh my God, it's 5%," while Iran is at 82%. She quotes an Iranian woman: I come to the market every day just to watch the prices go up, that's how I pass the time. She then places Iran alongside Ukraine — both are "war of choice" and miscalculation; Trump thought he could drive straight through Iran, Putin thought he could drive straight through Ukraine, and both found that people's resistance is both creative and determined.

Doucet gives the concrete mechanism: the Houthis control the western shore of the Red Sea and the islands in between, claiming they don't affect maritime traffic, but the previously de-escalating war between Saudi Arabia and Yemen has reignited; oil has risen past $108 a barrel; the Strait of Hormuz is completely frozen. The Iranians will not let go — they don't treat it merely as a bargaining chip but as a long-term chip, "They've weaponized the Strait of Hormuz." She points out that Trump repeatedly says "I didn't expect them to do this," but anyone who has done war-gaming will tell you the games always quickly move toward Iran controlling Hormuz.

When the Taliban required Afghan women to wear a burqa that leaves only the eyes exposed, Afghan women abroad pushed back, saying this is not traditional Afghanistan. Doucet points out that the burqa is locally called chadili, with an embroidered mesh; but in the same period women were also being educated at Kabul University. While writing her book she dug out a large number of old photographs and decided she had to tell this history well, so she tracked down a person living in the United States — whose first reaction was "The InterContinental, I love that hotel." Their first call lasted four hours, and the person drew the ground-floor plan of the hotel from memory, pointing out which room belonged to the German wife of the mayor of Kabul and which to an Indian.

points.h: Four hours of oral history, six months of silence
points.body: The second call lasted three hours, after which the person disappeared for about six months. The reason lay in Afghanistan's politics: in '73 the kingdom was ended by the first coup, and hotel employees were taken away for questioning — "Why do you work for an American hotel? Are you working for the CIA?" In '78 came the communist coup, people were thrown into prison, and she could only flee. Happy memories thus turned up sadness and pain. In the end Doucet called to ask for permission, and the person said: I can't appear in your book, it's too sad and too painful for me. Doucet's conclusion: a person writing a book can only get up the next day and find someone else to tell the story, and it will never be told as well.

points.h: Two trillion dollars bought a generation that knows its rights
points.body: Facing the challenge of "what was it all for," Doucet acknowledges that both sides made mistakes, that this should be a humbling lesson for all NATO allies, and that there will be a formal reckoning in the future. But she insists it was not all for nothing: twenty years of international intervention created space for the most educated and most connected generation in Afghanistan's history to grow up. She quotes Malala Yousafzai — even reading a book is an act of resistance — and says these girls know their rights, know that Islam gave them the right to education, know that girls around the world go to school while they cannot. "Not enough, but not zero."

points.h: The difference between hope and optimism is agency
points.body: Doucet says she could never tell hope and optimism apart until she read Gordon Brown's "The Future Starts With Us": optimism is wishful thinking, whereas hope is different because hope carries agency — you don't just make a wish, you actually work to bring it about. She says she doesn't have the privilege of "not needing to have hope"; the agency she has is fighting for an Afghan visa, listening to stories there, and telling those stories as well as she can; and everyone has their own bit of agency — some donate money, some help girls take classes online, some teach girls in Africa, some help South Sudan and Nicaragua, and some help struggling areas in Britain itself.
